content:
You don't need to tell your fat friend that they should consider losing weight, or that they should get on a GLP-1. Your fat friend already knows.

You might not need to tell your female friend who has disordered eating practices that they have an eating disorder. Your female friend has probably been in a middle school health class about how a significant fraction of girls will struggle with disordered eating in their lifetime. Your female friend has likely experienced many discourse cycles about disordered eating practices. But it's also very possible she's somehow convinced herself that her own case doesn't count for whatever reason. Or perhaps she's the kind of person who never took any of the PSAs seriously, and thinks that almond moms are behaving in perfectly acceptable ways.

You probably need to tell your male friend who is working out and cutting a lot that he might have an eating disorder. Disordered eating is not yet a concept that we have made readily available to men, despite men making up something like one quarter to one third of people with eating disorders.

The above set of claims has the following potential weaknesses:

  • Many people these days seem to have like only one to three friends, such that there isn't much of an information environment to model.
  • Many people find it very difficult to say true things when it is sufficiently awkward for them, such that obvious balls get dropped all of the time.

There is much additional throat clearing one can do about the above claims but I trust the reader to be able to generate them or to ask their preferred LLM for a list. I shall move on to my actual point.

In general, if you want to help someone who is dealing with some kind of difficult ongoing problem, it can be useful to develop a model of the information environment that your friend is living in.

The core move I want to articulate is to think about what the default, intuitive social response is1, and if you assess it to be oversupplied or otherwise unhelpful, to situate yourself somewhere a little less intuitive.

Sometimes the default, intuitive social response is good. If someone is going through a bad breakup, they will probably want a lot of support, as much as possible, so you might as well take them out for brunch and be another set of sympathetic ears as they pour out their woes to you.

Sometimes, the default, intuitive social response is good but only in limited quantities, and the general information environment way oversupplies it. It's probably good for your depressed, unemployed friend to know that it's likely beneficial for them to go back to school or to try to get a job or at least go to the gym. But the thing that they would find really helpful is not one more person telling them that or exhorting them to do so.

Sometimes the default, intuitive social response is actively bad and counterproductive. I write in detail about one case of this, when a friend is in an abusive relationship.

Often, what makes a social response the default, intuitive one is that it is a pareto optimal move that does not require much effort or risk on the part of the person performing it. This means that in situating yourself somewhere else often requires doing more work, or feeling more uncomfortable. You can offer to be gym buddies with your depressed friend, but this might incur more of a cost for you — for example, you will then need to then go to the gym yourself 😔.

Some of the most sophisticated social moves I have heard of require active strategizing and cooperation. For example, I know of one man who is the topic of a group chat he is not in. The group chat is for all of his friends and caretakers who are supporting him through his deep depression. It's a utilitarian, functional place, where people post sign-offs when they need to leave for work or sleep, and another person or two will offer to tag themselves in and note how long they'd be available for. I heard about this group chat at a brunch, and I don't know most of the people involved. I wonder how much intuition and how much strategy was required to build this chat.





  1. If you don't have a good sense of what the default, intuitive social response is, uh,,,, I don't really know if this is going to be a particularly useful post for you.↩
